content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper concerns the study of the spectral bias phenomenon. Few years ago, it was demonstrated that Relu-nets demonstrate a tendency to learn lower frequency functions firstly during the training, a phenomenon termed as spectral bias. The paper studies this phenomenon using the finite element method (FEM), while typically this is studied using the neural tangent kernel (NTK).  The authors observe that if the network structure is modified, the spectral bias is modified and indeed higher frequencies can be learned faster. In particular, the network is modified by using the Hat activation function is used for the analysis.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
* [+] The spectral bias (and the implicit bias in general) is an important aspect for understanding overparameterized neural networks. 

 * [+] The paper is well-written. 

 * [-] The analysis with vector inputs only considers two layer networks. 

 * [-] Similar phenomena about modifying the structure of the network have been observed in the literature but not discussed in the related work.   

 * [-] Even though solving PDEs is mentioned as a strong motivation for modifying the spectral bias, no such experiment is conducted in this work or in the literature.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
One core motivation in this work is that of using networks for solving PDEs, however no such empirical validation with the hat activation has emerged in the literature or is conducted in this work. 

Alleviating the spectral bias by modifying the structure of the network has also been studied in the literature, e.g. in “Fourier Features Let Networks Learn High Frequency Functions in Low Dimensional Domains” (NeurIPS’20) and “The Spectral Bias of Polynomial Neural Networks” (ICLR’22). The differences from those works should be discussed and also compare experimentally with those methods on alleviating the spectral bias. 

Does theorem 1 hold for every $n, j$? Or is $n$ considered only the maximum eigenvalue index?

I would recommend the authors to simplify the notation whenever possible, e.g. $a_i^l$ and $a_l$ are both used in page 5, making it harder to understand the manuscript. 

The experiments are rather weak, in the sense only one experiment with real-world data is included. Previous papers on the topic, e.g. see above, include several other experiments for empirical validation of the theoretical observations. 

Would it be possible to extend the analysis from two-layer networks to deep networks? 

Why is the hat activation special? Are there other activation functions with the same property? How about GeLU that is widely used in transformers or the swish activation function?
content.summary_of_the_review: I believe studying the spectral bias is important and this work offers a perspective through FEM, which is different from the related work. This can offer an insight on the relationship of width and spectral bias, however it seems to have few limitations, e.g. scaling to other architectures or deep nets. The paper could be further improved during the rebuttal and I would be willing to reconsider my rating when the comments above are addressed.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the spectral bias of neural networks with different activation functions. The author shows that when training the last layer of some shallow ReLU network over the population loss, the low-frequency components of the target function are picked up first, while replacing the activation function with a Hat function allows learning all frequency components simultaneously.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: This paper is mostly clear. There has not been much theoretical analysis for neural networks with Hat activation, and all results shown in the paper seem new.

Weakness: I have some concerns about both the significance of the theoretical results and the author's claims comparing Hat with ReLU activation
1. For the theoretical part, the setting is too restrictive: The task is fitting a 1-d function with a two-layer network, and the weights and the bias of the first layer are chosen to be fixed during training and only the last layer is being trained, and the author studies the population loss instead of an empirical loss. Therefore, the setting is far from what is done in practice: training all weights on empirical loss. Without justification of the practical relevance of the theory, the conclusion drawn from the theory might be misleading.

2. The setting for the theoretical part reduces the problem to nonlinear regression using some fixed basis functions. From this perspective, the results are not surprising, the scaled Hat $\sigma_H(n(x-\frac{i}{n}))$ can fit the high-frequency function easily as this basis function is a spike function on a very narrow interval $[\frac{i}{n},\frac{i+1}{n}]$. I acknowledge that there are some technical contributions in analyzing the spectrum of $M_\sigma$, but the current theory does not provide too much new insight.

3. The claim that Hat is better than ReLU in some applications is not well supported since the experiments are not good enough and to some extent misleading. Experiments E1 and E2 try to fit high-frequency 1d-function using either ReLU or Hat networks, in a noiseless setting with a fixed design on the sample, which naturally favors Hat for picking up high-frequency components quicker. But what if there is noise as in practice it generally does? I suspect the Hat network would do worse since it also picks up the high-frequency part from the noise while the ReLU network with proper early stopping, will result in a better fit to the ground truth. Additionally, Experiment E3 seems artificial, and the experiment in section 6.2 is unclear to me (what is the high-frequency noise being added?).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is mostly clear. The results are new.
content.summary_of_the_review: While presenting some interesting results, I think this paper still requires some improvement. The theoretical analysis should consider more realistic assumptions, and the claims should be supported by a set of more well-designed experiments.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper provides an analysis of the spectral bias of shallow, finite-width neural networks using either the ReLU or Hat activation functions, and shows that (in agreement with prior work) ReLU networks exhibit spectral bias whereas Hat networks do not. In other words, ReLU networks converge faster for function components of low frequency, whereas Hat networks converge at the same rate for all function components regardless of frequency. The paper complements this theoretical analysis of shallow networks (with fixed weights in the hidden layer) with experiments on deeper networks and in higher dimensions, including an image fitting task and a classification task on a binary subset of MNIST.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
- To the best of my knowledge, the analysis of the Hat function is novel and interesting, and may prove useful for certain applications in which spectral bias is undesirable.

Weaknesses/Limitations
- The design choices for what types of models to analyze is not clearly motivated. Why is the assumption of not training the hidden layer necessary? Why does Theorem 2 only consider ReLU networks (not Hat), and Theorem 3 only consider Hat networks (not ReLU)?
- Experiments are varied but still relatively small-scale, with the largest real dataset being a binary subset of MNIST. Fridovich-Keil et al 2021 suggests methods to extend to larger-scale experiments, but these may be too costly/slow to do during a rebuttal. Perhaps this can be mentioned as a suggestion for future work?
- The theoretical portions need some more explanation and double-checking. In particular, it is not clear how/where the notions of frequency introduced in section 3.1 are used in later sections. I'm also confused about what equations 11 and 12 are intending to convey, and I suspect there might be a typo in the line right below equation 12.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity
- Some of the bullet points under "weaknesses/limitations" contain clarity-related suggestions.
- It would be helpful to illustrate the Hat activation function alongside equation 5 where it is defined, perhaps in the same figure with a ReLU for comparison.
- The text in the figures should be larger; it is difficult to read without zooming in. Also, for multi-part figures the legend should either be replicated in each subplot, or placed outside all of the subplots.
- For Figure 3, I would suggest applying some exponential averaging to the curves so that the gap in convergence for different frequencies is easier to see, particularly for the bottom left subplot. The first row of this figure could be removed in my opinion, if space is needed.

Quality/Novelty
- The paper would benefit from a more thorough comparison to Rahaman et al 2019. That paper also studies the spectral bias of shallow, finite-width neural networks, but without the added assumption of not training the hidden-layer weights (to the best of my understanding). Rahaman et al. found an eigenvalue decay rate of $k^{-d-1}$, or $k^{-2}$ for specific directions. Here, however, the decay rate seems to be $k^{-4}$ according to Theorem 1; a discussion of this difference and why it arises would be helpful. 
- The connection to kernels is a bit unclear. Basri et al 2020 provide an analysis of spectral bias for ReLU networks using the NTK approximation, which bears similarity to the arguments made here. My understanding is that the main difference is that the current analysis allows for finite-width models, but does not train the hidden layer weights. Is this correct? What added insights come from this analysis compared to that provided in Basri et al? 
- Relatedly, a similar NTK analysis is provided in https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.10739 for the case of sinusoidal activation function; a discussion of any similarities and differences between this and the Hat activation would benefit the current paper. My understanding is that ReLU networks have fixed spectral bias, the sinusoidal activation in https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.10739 allows for a tunable spectral bias, and Hat networks have no spectral bias--if this is correct then it would be helpful for readers to know so they can choose the appropriate activation function for their task.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall I think the paper makes a valuable contribution, particularly in its theoretical and experimental study of the Hat function and its influence on spectral bias of neural networks. However, I think the paper needs a more thorough discussion of a few highly related works, and some edits to the math and figures to improve readability.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the "spectral bias" of neural networks (NNs), and proposes a theoretical analysis for shallow NNs without biases: the authors prove that there is no spectral bias when using the "Hat activation function", and there is one when using ReLU. They also propose experiments on synthetic datasets to support their claims.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths

A theoretical analysis of the spectral bias is helpful to understand the behavior of NNs during training. 

The authors indicate how to obtain theoretical results about the implicit bias.

## Weaknesses 

### Overstatement of the claims

In the abstract, the introduction, and in the list of the contributions, the authors omit the very restrictive condition of their main theorems: Theorem 3 only applies to shallow NNs without biases; Theorem 1 only applies to shallow NNs with constant biases and input weights ($= 1$). These very restrictive conditions *must* appear in the abstract and in the contributions. Otherwise, the claims would be overstated *by omission*: by omitting these conditions, the authors let the reader think that the result is very general, which is far from being the case.

This is a major issue.

### Citations

According to the paper, the authors have chosen to use the "Hat activation function" because it showed better performance than ReLU in [A]. But, after taking a look to [A], it appears that Hat is better than ReLU, but with an extremely small margin. Averaged on 3 runs (!), the error rate decreases by ~10 % on MNIST, and by less than 2 % on other datasets. Naturally, it is impossible to obtain meaningful confidence intervals with 3 runs per setup. Despite [A] has been published to ICCS, its results remain doubtful and not backed by a strong experimental validation process. 

Besides, the authors of [A] cite the present paper to justify their own use of the Hat function. So, the authors of the present paper cite [A] to justify their use of the Hat function, and the authors of [A] cite this paper to do the same. This cyclical justification is not advisable.

Note: cyclical citations are not a problem in general, and they are common when *similar works* are pre-published by different teams in the same period of time. This is not the case here.

So, I would recommend not to cite [A] at all (since their results are very weak). At the very least, [A] may be cited, but only to report the use of the Hat function, and without backing their claims.

### Arbitrary choices

After Eqn. (5), the authors say: "The Hat activation function is not scale invariant. As a result, we will also consider more generally a
scaled Hat function $\sigma_{H}(\alpha \cdot)$ as an activation function". I do not understand why "not scale invariant" implies "we consider scaled activation function". For instance, $\tanh$ is not scale invariant, but its scaled version $\tanh(\alpha \cdot)$ is not widely used.

Experiment 2. The authors choose different initialization distribution, different learnings, and different learning rates schedules for NNs with ReLU and with Hat. The authors should justify these choices. Otherwise, how would the reader check the fairness or the comparison between ReLU and Hat?

Experiment 3. Moreover, the initialization distributions chosen by the authors for Experiment 2 are inconsistent with the choices they make for Experiment 3, where the same distribution has been chosen for ReLU and for Hat. This inconsistency should be solved. The authors may use the works of [B] to have a widely known, theoretically backed initialization procedure (and they can adapt it to their Hat function).

## References

[A] *CNNs with Compact Activation Function*, Wang et al., 2022.

[B] *Delving deep into rectifiers: Surpassing human-level performance on imagenet classification*, He et al., 2015.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
## Clarity

The paper is difficult to follow.

Theorem 1, Eqn. (9) and (10). These results are asymptotic. But according to what? Do we have $n \rightarrow \infty$? Both $n \rightarrow \infty$ and $j \rightarrow \infty$ with $j/n = \text{constant}$?

Theorem 1, Eqn. (10). The big-O notation is ambiguous in this case, and the conclusion of "uniformly bounded" is unclear. If $(\lambda_n/\lambda_j))_{n}$ is bounded by $K_j$, we cannot directly conclude that the sequence of $(K_j)_j$ is itself bounded. 

Issues:
* the authors should use "citep" instead of "cite": parentheses should be used for every citation;

## Quality

I did not check the math. However, I am sure that the main results (Theorem 1 and 3), if they are made clearer, could be very useful in the field of NN training dynamics.

## Novelty

I am not aware of the literature about the spectral bias. Though, as far as I know, the contribution is novel and can be useful for further works about the learning dynamic of deep NNs with biases.

## Reproducibility

Though the authors provide their hyperparameters and training procedures, they do not explain their choices. So,  their results are not *fully* reproducible: how did they choose the initialization distribution of the parameters? the learning rate? the learning rate schedules?
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Thank you for your reviews
content.comment:
We wanted to thank the reviewers for their helpful comments. Based upon these comments, we are currently working on improving the empirical experiments presented in the paper to validate the theoretical results. Unfortunately, we have not been able to complete this in time to meet the revision deadline and as a result have decided to withdraw our paper.

We only wanted to make one comment regarding the accusation made by reviewer hgY9 that we intentionally misrepresented our results ("the good faith of the authors could be involved"). We very strongly disagree with the assessment that our abstract and introduction misrepresent our results. In our paper we only claim that our results provide a"`theoretical explanation" for the spectral bias, not, as the reviewer seemed to interpret, a proof that the spectral bias holds for deep networks in all situations. We do believe that our results, although they only hold under very restrictive assumptions, provide significant insight into why the spectral bias is occurring. The reviewer may disagree with this, which we accept. However, from our perspective, all theoretical results in deep learning make highly unrealistic and restrictive assumptions and then argue that their results provide some intuition into what is happening in practice. This is exactly what we do and we strongly disagree with the accusation that we are over-selling our results.
